title: Metamorphism
intro: Metamorphism means a rock is cooked, squeezed or soaked while it stays SOLID, and turns into a new rock. Learn: the starting rock (protolith), the 3 agents (heat, pressure, fluids), the 5 processes, foliated vs nonfoliated rocks, the grade ladder (slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss), and where each kind of metamorphism happens.

boxes.text: Why must the rock stay solid? If it melts, it cools into an igneous rock, which is a different path in the rock cycle. In metamorphism, atoms shuffle around inside the solid crystals, like people rearranging seats in a full theatre without anyone leaving.
PROTOlith = the FIRST rock. Metamorphic = the Meta-MORPH rock: it changes FORM, like a Transformer.
Protolith means the rock BEFORE it is metamorphosed (midterm Q11). It is NOT the rock before it is weathered. Any rock type can be a protolith, not only sedimentary rock.

steps.title: Solid-state alteration
bullets: **Metamorphic rocks** result from **solid-state alteration** of preexisting rocks: an older rock is changed while it stays solid.
This folded, banded rock is an example.

img.alt: Steep canyon walls of banded pink and grey rock, with notes defining metamorphic rocks and protoliths.

steps.title: Meta, morphe and protolith
bullets: **Meta** = beyond/change and **morphe** = form, so metamorphism means a change of form.
The rock you start with is the **protolith** (proto = first, lithos = rock), also called the **parent rock**. It can be igneous, sedimentary, or even already metamorphic.

img.alt: Folded, broken grey rock with a pale band, with notes about what changes and how fast.

steps.title: What changes, and how fast
bullets: Protoliths change in **texture** (how the grains look and line up) and **mineralogy** (which minerals are there).
Causes: temperature, pressure, tectonic stress, and the amount of reactive water. The change is **slow** and happens in the solid state.
Mineral example: **red shale** (quartz, clay, iron oxide) becomes **gneiss** (quartz, feldspar, biotite, garnet).

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The rock cycle: metamorphic rock forms from other rocks by **burial, heating and remetamorphism**, without melting.
Metamorphism is NOT melting. Melting makes igneous rock.

boxes.text: Why do minerals line up? When a rock is squeezed in one main direction, flat crystals turn or grow sideways to the squeeze, like sheets of paper lying flat in a stack under a heavy weight. The details are in the Differential Stress section.
Foliation comes from Latin folium = LEAF. Think of pages or leaves in a stack, all parallel.

Two rock close-ups: one with randomly placed quartz and feldspar, one with feldspar crystals lined up roughly parallel.

steps.title: Texture before and after
bullets: Under a microscope the protolith has fossil fragments.
After metamorphism the fragments are replaced by big, new **calcite crystals**. The texture changed.

img.alt: Two rock close-ups: one with randomly placed quartz and feldspar, one with feldspar crystals lined up roughly parallel.

steps.title: What foliation looks like
bullets: Metamorphism often gives the new rock a **foliation**: a **planar fabric** (a flat, sheet-like pattern) that cuts through the rock.
Left rock: quartz and feldspar are placed randomly. Right rock: feldspar crystals are roughly parallel to one line.

img.alt: A large boulder with alternating light and dark bands.

steps.title: Two ways to make foliation
bullets: Foliation is made by the **alignment of platy minerals** (like micas).
It can also come from the creation of **alternating light and dark bands**, as in this boulder.

boxes.text: Why do high pressures make new minerals? Squeezing pushes atoms closer, so the rock prefers minerals that pack atoms more tightly (denser ones). If the formula stays the same it is a phase change; if elements are swapped around to make different minerals it is neocrystallization.
Re-crystallization = same crystal again (same mineral, new size). Neo = NEW mineral. Phase change = same formula, new shape (like the same Lego bricks rebuilt into a different model).

Kyanite to sillimanite is a PHASE CHANGE (same Al2SiO5), not neocrystallization (practice Q40). Pressure solution and plastic deformation both make elliptical grains: pressure solution dissolves and regrows, plastic deformation bends the grain without dissolving.

steps.title: Phase change
bullets: **Phase change**: new minerals form with the **same chemical formula but a different crystal structure**.
Example: andalusite to kyanite to sillimanite (all three are Al2SiO5).

img.alt: Dark red almandine garnet crystals scattered through fine-grained grey rock.

steps.title: Pressure and denser minerals
bullets: Pressure rises with depth at **270 to 300 bars per km** (1 bar is about 1 atm = 14.7 psi). Most metamorphism happens at **2 to 12 kbar** (2,000 to 12,000 bars).
Higher pressure packs atoms tighter, favouring **denser minerals**, so phase changes or neocrystallization happen.
The photo shows almandine garnet **porphyroblasts** (big crystals in a fine matrix).

img.alt: Diagram: round grains in the original rock become flattened, elliptical grains, with dissolving at pressed contacts and new growth in between.

steps.title: Pressure solution
bullets: **Pressure solution**: grains partly **dissolve where their surfaces press together**. The ions travel in a thin water film and **reprecipitate** elsewhere. It needs a little water.
Spherical grains become elliptical.
**Plastic deformation** also makes grains elliptical: grains soften and **change shape without breaking**, like plastic, when squeezed or sheared at high T and P.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Recrystallization**: minerals change **size and shape** by dissolving and regrowing crystals. The **mineral does not change**. Example: limestone to marble.

**Neocrystallization** (metamorphic reaction): old minerals become unstable and react; elements are recycled into a **new mineral assemblage**. Example: shale to garnet mica schist (clay and quartz become quartz, garnet, mica).

sections.title: Agents: heat, pressure, differential stress, fluids

boxes.text: Why does uneven stress make foliation but even pressure does not? Even pressure squeezes a rock the same from every side, so nothing lines up. A bigger push from one side flattens grains and aligns flat minerals sideways to it. Pressure mainly changes which minerals form; differential stress mainly changes texture.
PRESSURE = a swimmer deep in water, squeezed from every side equally. DIFFERENTIAL STRESS = pressing a ball of dough between your palms, pushing harder in one direction.
Do not mix up pressure and differential stress. Pressure is equal in all directions; differential stress is greater in one direction. Also: compression pushes together, tension pulls apart.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Equal in all directions; rises with depth

steps.title: The four agents
bullets: The **agents of metamorphism** are **heat (T)**, **pressure (P)**, **compression and shear**, and **hydrothermal (hot water) fluids**.
Hydrothermal fluids are hot water with dissolved ions and volatiles. They **accelerate metamorphism**.
The fluids are mostly H2O and CO2. They react with protolith minerals or add new elements.

img.alt: A hand pressing on a lump of dough-like rock: first squeezed from all sides, then sheared sideways.

steps.title: Pressure, stress and shear
bullets: **Pressure** is **equal in all directions**. **Differential stress** is greater in one direction, like dough under a heavy weight on top (vertical compression) instead of an even squeeze.
**Normal stress** acts perpendicular to a surface. **Compression** pushes together; **tension** pulls apart.
**Shear stress**: forces act in opposite directions along a surface, like a hand pushing the top of dough sideways.

img.alt: Diagram: a round (equant) grain turns into a cigar-shaped (elongate) or flat (platy) grain under stress.

steps.title: Grain shapes under stress
bullets: Compression and shear plus high T and P make minerals and rocks **change shape without breaking**. Crystals line up at a right angle to the compression.
**Equant** grains are about equal in all dimensions. After stress they can become inequant (dimensions not all the same).
**Elongate** grains are cigar-shaped (e.g. staurolite); **platy** grains are pancake-like (e.g. micas).

sections.title: Foliated rocks and the grade ladder

boxes.text: Why does the sequence go slate to phyllite to schist to gneiss? More heat and pressure let the mica crystals grow larger step by step, so grains go from too tiny to see (slate) to silky sheen (phyllite) to visible flakes (schist) to coarse separated bands (gneiss).
Order of grain size and grade: SLATE, PHYLLITE, SCHIST, GNEISS. 'Some People Sure Grow' (S, P, S, G). Gneiss is pronounced like 'nice'.

Practice Q35 wants the grade order slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss (not schist before phyllite). Practice Q36: slaty cleavage is PERPENDICULAR to the compression, and not always parallel to bedding. Foliation comes from metamorphism, bedding comes from sedimentary processes.

bullets: **Foliated** rocks have a planar fabric. The grade ladder from shale runs: **slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss**, then migmatite at the extreme.
**Metaconglomerate** is a metamorphosed conglomerate: a foliated rock with stretched pebbles.

img.alt: Diagram of slaty cleavage forming at right angles to the squeeze, and a worker splitting slate into roofing tiles.

steps.title: Slate and slaty cleavage
bullets: **Slate** is a fine-grained, **low-grade** metamorphic shale with a distinct foliation called **slaty cleavage**.
Slaty cleavage develops **perpendicular to compression** by parallel alignment of clays. It does not have to line up with the original bedding.
Slate breaks along the foliation, making roofing tiles.

img.alt: A banded gneiss with a coin for scale, and a diagram of felsic and mafic minerals separating into bands over time.

steps.title: Gneiss and migmatite
bullets: **Gneiss** has distinct **compositional bands**: **light** bands of **felsic** minerals (quartz and feldspar) alternate with **dark** bands of **mafic** minerals (biotite or amphibole).
Banding develops by **metamorphic differentiation**: felsic minerals dissolve, ions migrate and regrow in one band; mafic minerals do the same in another.
**Migmatite** is **partly melted gneiss**, with features of both igneous and metamorphic rocks. Light felsic bands formed from melt; dark mafic bands stayed solid.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Phyllite** is fine-grained and mica-rich, formed by further metamorphism of slate. It has a **silky sheen** called **phyllitic luster**.
**Schist** has fine to coarse crystals with **larger micas**, so it is **medium- to high-grade**. Foliation from big micas is called **schistosity**.

boxes.text: Why is marble not foliated? It is basically one mineral (calcite) with no flat minerals to line up. Heat just lets the crystals grow bigger and interlock in all directions.
Quartzite = QUARTZ sandstone; Marble = limestone 'Mar-ble, Lime-stone'. Match the sedimentary parent by its main mineral: quartz to quartzite, calcite to marble.
Midterm Q19: the nonfoliated rock in the list is quartzite, not phyllite, gneiss, slate or schist. Midterm Q18: the metamorphic equivalent of limestone is marble.

images.alt: Orange layered sandstone outcrop next to a hard grey quartzite sample with a coin for scale.
A grey limestone outcrop, a marble quarry with pale blocks, and a marble sculpture.

img.alt: Orange layered sandstone outcrop next to a hard grey quartzite sample with a coin for scale.

steps.title: Quartzite
bullets: **Quartzite** is metamorphic **quartz sandstone**. The sand grains recrystallize and fuse into a rock that is **hard, glassy, and resistant**.
Quartzite breaks across the grains; sandstone breaks around them.

img.alt: A grey limestone outcrop, a marble quarry with pale blocks, and a marble sculpture.

steps.title: Marble
bullets: **Marble** is coarsely crystalline **calcite or dolomite** from a **limestone or dolostone** protolith.
Marble fizzes with dilute HCl (calcite) and is softer than quartzite.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Nonfoliated** rocks lack a planar fabric. Reasons: no strong compression, mostly **equant** minerals, or **no platy minerals**. They usually have just one mineral.
**Hornfels** is a fine-grained rock from the **baked margin** of a plutonic intrusion, often extremely hard and durable. See contact metamorphism.

sections.title: Grade, heat, index minerals and facies

boxes.text: Why is hornfels high T and low P while blueschist is high P and low T? Hornfels forms next to hot magma close to the surface, so there is lots of heat but little weight. Blueschist forms in a cold slab pushed deep down quickly, so there is lots of weight but little heat. The geothermal gradient (how fast temperature rises with depth) is high for hornfels and low for blueschist.

Hornfels = HOT and shallow (Hot + Few). BLUEschist = BLUE and cold: low T, high P. Index minerals going up: 'Cool Mice Bite Great Stinky Kitty Slippers' = Chlorite, Muscovite, Biotite, Garnet, Staurolite, Kyanite, Sillimanite.

Midterm Q12: hornfels = high temperature and low pressure; blueschist = high pressure and low temperature. In practice the pressure gradient with depth is almost the same everywhere; it is the temperature gradient that varies a lot. Grade is about intensity of change, not about which rock it is.

steps.title: Temperature and heat sources
bullets: Metamorphism occurs between **250 degrees C and 850 degrees C**. The depth to this temperature depends on the tectonic setting.
Sources of heat: the **geothermal gradient**, magmatic intrusions, and tectonic compression.

img.alt: Chart of shale and sandstone changing into slate, phyllite and quartzite, schist and gneiss, with the minerals that appear at each grade.

steps.title: The grade ladder
bullets: **Metamorphic grade**: **low grade = slight** change, **high grade = intense** change. More T and P means higher grade.
Shale and sandstone grow into slate, then phyllite and quartzite, then schist, then gneiss as grade goes from low to high.
Shale index minerals in grade order: **clay, chlorite, muscovite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite**.

img.alt: Chart with temperature increasing to the right and pressure increasing downward, placing hornfels, slate, schist, gneiss, migmatite and blueschist.

steps.title: Where each rock forms
bullets: Temperature goes right and pressure goes down. **Hornfels** is on the high-T, low-P side; **blueschist** is on the high-P, low-T side.
Schist and gneiss sit in between, and migmatite is at the highest grade.
Contact metamorphism runs at low pressure, mountain-belt metamorphism at moderate to high P, and subduction metamorphism at high P and low T. Wet granite and wet basalt start to melt at high T.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The minerals that form depend on the **protolith composition** and the **grade**. Basalt makes greenschist, amphibolite and mafic granulite. Shale makes slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss.

A **metamorphic facies** is a set of **mineral assemblages** that indicate a certain **range of P and T** (diagenesis, zeolite, greenschist, amphibolite, granulite, hornfels, blueschist, eclogite). **Index minerals** show the grade of a rock and make maps of **metamorphic zones**; a New England map colours zones from biotite-chlorite (low grade) to cordierite (high grade).

sections.title: Types of metamorphism and contact metamorphism

boxes.text: Why is hornfels usually not foliated? It forms mainly from heat. With no strong differential stress, there is nothing to align the minerals into a layer.
Think of toast: the part touching the toaster (the pluton) is most baked (highest grade); the far end of the bread is barely changed.
Slide 64 asks what contact metamorphism produces: hornfels (not 'imafels', 'hullafels' or 'granofels', which are joke answers). Hornfels is an intrusion-baked metamorphic rock, NOT an igneous rock.

images.alt: A map and block diagram of a granodiorite pluton in Maine ringed by low-, intermediate- and high-grade hornfels, with slate beyond.
Block diagram of an igneous pluton surrounded by bands of hornfels, with clay, brick, pottery and porcelain drawn above.
Close-up of dark, fine-grained hornfels with pale patches.

img.alt: A map and block diagram of a granodiorite pluton in Maine ringed by low-, intermediate- and high-grade hornfels, with slate beyond.

bullets: **Contact (thermal) metamorphism** is caused by heat from a **magma body intruding host rock**.
It is **high temperature, low pressure**. Fine-grained shale and basalt recrystallize to hornfels; sandstone becomes quartzite and limestone becomes marble.

img.alt: Block diagram of an igneous pluton surrounded by bands of hornfels, with clay, brick, pottery and porcelain drawn above.

steps.title: The contact aureole
bullets: Contact heat makes a **contact aureole**: zoned bands of alteration, **high grade near the pluton** to **low grade away from it**. The zones are low-grade, intermediate and high-grade hornfels.
Metamorphism is like going from **clay to brick to pottery to porcelain** as you add heat.

img.alt: Close-up of dark, fine-grained hornfels with pale patches.

steps.title: Hornfels
bullets: **Hornfels** is a fine-grained, hard, durable rock from the **baked margin** of an intrusion.
It is **not foliated**: the rock may not have had compression, may be mostly equant minerals, or lacks platy minerals.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The main **types of metamorphism** and their settings: **Thermal** (heating by a plutonic intrusion), **Burial** (deep burial in a basin), **Dynamic** (shearing in a fault zone), **Regional** (P and T change due to orogenesis), **Hydrothermal** (alteration by hot-water leaching), **Subduction** (high P and low T), **Shock** (extreme high P from a bolide impact).

boxes.text: Why breccia on top and mylonite below? Cold shallow rock is brittle like a cracker: it breaks into angular pieces. Hot deep rock is ductile like warm taffy: it stretches and smears, and the grains get smaller.
BRECCIA = BROKEN (brittle, shallow). MYLONITE = MELTED-LOOKING SMEAR like taffy (ductile, deep, 15 km+).

Practice Q38: granite sheared at 25 km is deeper than 15 km, so the answer is MYLONITE, not fault breccia. Also, the textbook mentions rock flour and cataclasite at shallow levels; the slide only uses 'fault breccia'. Use the slide's wording.

Two cross sections: Point A as sediment at the surface (20 degrees C, 1 bar), then about 15 km deep after a collision (450 degrees C, 6 kbar).
The same before-and-after cross sections drawn over a photo of banded metamorphic rock.

bullets: **Dynamic metamorphism** is breakage of rock by **shearing in a fault zone**.
**Shallow crust (0 to 15 km)**: rocks are **brittle** and crush to **fault breccia**.
**Deeper crust (15 km and deeper)**: rocks are **ductile** and smear **like taffy** to form **mylonite**, which has **very tiny grains**.

img.alt: Two cross sections: Point A as sediment at the surface (20 degrees C, 1 bar), then about 15 km deep after a collision (450 degrees C, 6 kbar).

steps.title: Regional: before and after
bullets: Point A starts as sediment near the surface at 20 degrees C and 1 bar.
After the collision it is about 15 km deep at **450 degrees C and 6 kbar**.

img.alt: The same before-and-after cross sections drawn over a photo of banded metamorphic rock.

steps.title: Why regional makes the most rock
bullets: **Regional (dynamothermal) metamorphism**: tectonic collisions deform huge **mobile belts** hundreds to thousands of km long. Directed compression buries rocks deeply, where the geothermal gradient and plutons heat them.
It creates **more metamorphic rock than any other mechanism**.

sections.title: Hydrothermal, subduction, burial, shock

boxes.text: Why blueschist in subduction? The cold ocean slab sinks faster than it can warm up, so pressure climbs quickly but temperature stays low. Rock is a good insulator, so the slab heats slowly.
BLUEschist = BLUE and COLD, from SUBduction. Black smokers = the ocean-ridge 'chimneys' for hydrothermal change.

Slide 63: blueschist goes with ocean crust subducting beneath a continent (not collisions, rifting, spreading or transform). Regional metamorphism is collisions; blueschist is subduction. Also do not confuse hornfels (hot, low P) with blueschist (cold, high P).

steps.title: Hydrothermal at ridges
bullets: At **mid-ocean ridges**, cold seawater seeps into fractured crust, is heated by magma, reacts with the **mafic rock (basalt)**, and exits through **black smokers**.
The mafic rock is metamorphically altered. The outcrop shown is greenstone (metamorphosed pillow basalt).

img.alt: Block diagram of a subduction zone showing blueschist forming in an accretionary prism and contact metamorphism near the volcanoes.

steps.title: Subduction and blueschist
bullets: Trenches and accretionary prisms have a **low geothermal gradient**. This produces **low T, high P** rock called **blueschist**.
Blueschist is named for **glaucophane**, a blue amphibole mineral.

img.alt: Aerial view of a large round impact crater.

steps.title: Shock metamorphism
bullets: A comet or asteroid impact makes **extremely high pressure and heat** that vaporizes rock, makes shock minerals, or makes high-pressure minerals.
Shock minerals include the quartz polymorphs coesite and stishovite, plus shatter cones and tektites.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Burial** metamorphism: P and T increase as sediments are buried in a basin by the weight of overburden and the geothermal gradient. **Below about 8 to 15 km**, metamorphic changes replace diagenetic effects.

sections.title: Back to the surface and shields

boxes.text: Why can we see once-deep gneiss at the surface? The mountains were squeezed up, spread out, and then eroded for a very long time. What is left on top of the old belt is the deep root.
Recipe: VISE (squeeze up), CHEESE in the sun (collapse), RASP (erosion) = deep rock arrives at the top.

images.alt: Three-stage diagram: continents squeeze rock up like dough in a vise, the thick belt collapses like cheese in the sun, and erosion removes the top like a rasp.
World map labelling the ancient shields on each continent.

img.alt: Three-stage diagram: continents squeeze rock up like dough in a vise, the thick belt collapses like cheese in the sun, and erosion removes the top like a rasp.

bullets: **Exhumation** brings deep metamorphic rocks back up. As continents squeeze together in a collision, rock is pushed up like dough in a vise.
Uplift thickens the crust; the softened deep rock then **collapses and thins**, like a block of cheese in the hot sun.
**Erosion** then grinds away the top and exposes deeper rock, like a rasp on wood.

img.alt: World map labelling the ancient shields on each continent.

bullets: **Shields** are large regions of ancient high-grade metamorphic rock in continental interiors, the eroded remnants of **orogenic belts**.
They form the **basement** under sedimentary cover over much of the world. Examples on the map: Canadian, Baltic, Siberian, African, Australian and more.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Many metamorphic rocks are dry**, which prevents **retrograde reactions** (the rock does not change back as it cools).

sections.title: Check questions
bullets: Which is NOT metamorphic? Gneiss, phyllite, schist and slate are metamorphic; **basalt is igneous**.
Which IS metamorphic? Quartzite and marble, so the answer is both. Granite is igneous, sandstone is sedimentary.
Blueschist goes with **ocean crust subducting beneath a continent**.
Contact metamorphism typically produces **hornfels**.

boxes.text: Metamorphic names to avoid mixing up: sandstone (sedimentary) vs quartzite (metamorphic); granite (igneous) vs gneiss (metamorphic); basalt (igneous) vs greenstone (metamorphosed basalt).

cards.back: A rock that formed by solid-state alteration of a preexisting rock (protolith), without melting.
The preexisting (parent) rock that is altered during metamorphism. It can be igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic.
Meta = beyond/change; morphe = form. Metamorphism = change of form.

cards.front: What are the five types of change that make metamorphic rocks?
cards.back: Recrystallization, phase change, metamorphic reaction (neocrystallization), pressure solution, plastic deformation.
cards.short: Recrystallization, phase change, neocrystallization, pressure solution, plastic deformation

cards.back: Minerals change size and shape by dissolution and growth of crystals; the identity of the mineral does not change. Example: limestone to marble.
cards.short: Same mineral, new size and shape

cards.back: New minerals form with the same chemical formula but a different crystal structure, e.g. andalusite, kyanite, sillimanite (all Al2SiO5).
Protolith minerals become unstable and react, recycling elements into a new mineral assemblage. Example: shale to garnet mica schist.
Grains partly dissolve where their surfaces press together; ions move in a thin water film and reprecipitate. Needs a little water.
cards.short: Dissolves at pressed contacts, regrows nearby

cards.back: Mineral grains soften and change shape without breaking when squeezed or sheared at high T and P.
cards.short: Grains bend like plastic without breaking

cards.front: How fast does pressure rise with depth in the crust?
cards.back: 270 to 300 bars per km. Metamorphism mostly occurs at 2 to 12 kbar (2,000 to 12,000 bars).
Heat (T), pressure (P), compression and shear, and hydrothermal (hot water) fluids.
Stress that is greater in one direction. It differs from pressure, which is equal in all directions.
Both are normal stress (perpendicular to a surface). Compression is push-together; tension is pull-apart.
Equant: about equal in all dimensions. Elongate: cigar-shaped (staurolite). Platy: pancake-like (micas).
Hot water with dissolved ions and volatiles; it accelerates metamorphism.
cards.short: Hot water that speeds up metamorphism

cards.back: A parallel planar fabric (Latin folium = leaf) made by aligned platy minerals or alternating light and dark bands.
cards.short: Parallel planar fabric through a rock

cards.back: Fine-grained, low-grade metamorphic shale with slaty cleavage, which develops perpendicular to compression. Breaks into roofing tiles.
cards.short: Low grade, slaty cleavage, roofing tiles

cards.back: Fine-grained, mica-rich rock formed from slate, with a silky sheen called phyllitic luster.
Fine to coarse rock with larger micas (medium to high grade); foliation from large mica crystals is called schistosity.
Rock with distinct compositional bands: light felsic bands (quartz, feldspar) alternate with dark mafic bands (biotite or amphibole).
cards.short: Light felsic and dark mafic bands

cards.back: A partially melted gneiss with features of both igneous and metamorphic rocks. Light bands formed from melt; dark bands stayed solid.

cards.front: Order of increasing grade for a shale protolith
cards.back: Shale, then slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss (then migmatite at the extreme).
Nonfoliated metamorphic quartz sandstone; grains recrystallize and fuse into a hard, glassy, resistant rock.
Nonfoliated, coarsely crystalline calcite or dolomite from a limestone or dolostone protolith.
A metamorphosed conglomerate.
Fine-grained, hard, durable nonfoliated rock from the baked margin of plutonic intrusions (contact metamorphism).
The geothermal gradient, magmatic intrusions, and tectonic compression. Metamorphism occurs at about 250 to 850 degrees C.
Amount of metamorphic change: low grade is slight, high grade is intense.
Minerals that show the metamorphic grade of a rock and are used to map metamorphic zones, e.g. chlorite (low) up to sillimanite (high).
A set of mineral assemblages that indicates a certain range of pressure and temperature conditions.
cards.short: Mineral assemblages for a P-T range

cards.back: Heat from a magma body intruding host rock; makes a contact aureole zoned from high grade near the pluton to low grade away.
Shearing in a fault zone: fault breccia in the brittle shallow crust (0-15 km), mylonite in the ductile deeper crust (15 km+).
Very fine-grained rock formed by ductile shearing (smeared like taffy) in fault zones deeper than 15 km.
Collisions deform huge mobile belts; rocks are buried and heated. Makes more metamorphic rock than any other mechanism.
At mid-ocean ridges, seawater seeps in, is heated, reacts with basalt and exits through black smokers.
Low-T, high-P rock named after glaucophane (a blue amphibole); forms in trenches and accretionary prisms where the geothermal gradient is low.
P and T rise as sediments are buried in a basin. Below about 8 to 15 km, metamorphic changes replace diagenetic effects.
Comet or asteroid impact makes extremely high pressure and heat; vaporizes rock or makes shock and high-pressure minerals.
Return of metamorphic rocks to the surface: uplift, collapse and thinning of thickened crust, then erosion removes upper material.
cards.short: Deep rocks brought back to surface

cards.back: Large regions of ancient high-grade metamorphic rock in continental interiors; eroded orogenic belts that form basement under sedimentary cover.

quiz.q: "Protolith" is a term that refers to ...?
options: a type of fossil from the Phanerozoic
the type of rock before it is weathered
an early formed sedimentary rock type
the type of rock before it is metamorphosed
quiz.why: A protolith is the preexisting (parent) rock that gets altered during metamorphism. It can be igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five types of change that can make metamorphic rocks?
quiz.why: Metamorphism happens in the solid state. Melting makes magma and then igneous rock. The five types are recrystallization, phase change, neocrystallization, pressure solution and plastic deformation.

quiz.q: In a metamorphic rock, kyanite converts to sillimanite (both Al2SiO5). Which metamorphic process is this?
quiz.why: Same chemical formula but a different crystal structure is the definition of a phase change.

quiz.q: A limestone turns into marble, and the calcite crystals just grow larger and interlock. Which process is mainly responsible?
quiz.why: The mineral (calcite) stays the same; only crystal size and shape change by dissolution and regrowth. That is recrystallization (limestone to marble is the classic example).

quiz.q: Why is shale becoming garnet mica schist an example of neocrystallization and NOT recrystallization?
options: The same minerals just got bigger
Old minerals (clay, quartz) reacted to form new minerals (garnet, mica)
Only the crystal structure changed, not the formula
Grains dissolved only where they touched
quiz.why: Neocrystallization makes NEW minerals from unstable old ones by chemical reactions. Recrystallization keeps the same mineral.

quiz.q:
Which of the following statements are correct?
I. Pressure is equal in all directions.
II. Differential stress is greater in one direction than in others.
III. Tension is a push-together normal stress.
quiz.why: Statements I and II are the definitions of pressure and differential stress. III is wrong: compression is push-together, tension is pull-apart.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of increasing metamorphic grade for a shale protolith?
quiz.why: Grain size and grade increase step by step: slate (fine), phyllite (silky), schist (visible micas), gneiss (coarse bands).

quiz.q: How is slaty cleavage oriented?
options: Perpendicular to the direction of maximum compression
Always parallel to the original bedding
Parallel to the direction of maximum compression
quiz.why: Slaty cleavage develops perpendicular to compression by parallel alignment of clays. It does not have to match bedding.

quiz.q: Many metamorphic rocks have a foliation. Which of the following is a metamorphic rock that does NOT have a foliation?
quiz.why: Quartzite is a nonfoliated rock made of recrystallized quartz. Slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss are foliated.

quiz.q:
Which of the following protolith-to-rock pairs are correct?
I. Quartz sandstone to quartzite
II. Limestone to marble
III. Conglomerate to metaconglomerate
quiz.why: All three pairs are correct: quartz sandstone to quartzite, limestone to marble, conglomerate to metaconglomerate.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT true of gneiss?
options: Light bands of quartz and feldspar alternate with dark bands of biotite or amphibole
It forms at high metamorphic grade
It is nonfoliated and has no banding
Partial melting of it produces a migmatite
quiz.why: Gneiss is foliated and has compositional banding. The false statement is that it is nonfoliated without banding.

quiz.q: Why is hornfels from a contact aureole usually NOT foliated?
options: It forms mainly from heat, without strong differential stress to align the minerals
It forms at very high pressure
quiz.why: Foliation needs compression or shear to align minerals. Hornfels is baked by magma heat, with little directed stress and often equant minerals.

quiz.q: Granite is sheared in a fault zone at a depth of 25 km. What rock is most likely produced?
quiz.why: Below about 15 km rocks are ductile and smear like taffy into mylonite. Fault breccia forms in the brittle shallow crust (0 to 15 km).

quiz.q: Blueschist (high pressure, low temperature) forms in subduction zones because:
options: Subduction zones have a high geothermal gradient
The cold slab sinks faster than it can heat up, so pressure rises much faster than temperature (a low geothermal gradient)
quiz.why: Trenches and accretionary prisms have a low geothermal gradient. The slab sinks quickly and stays cool, so P rises faster than T.

quiz.q: Different types of metamorphosed terrains are associated with different pressure and temperature gradients. The hornfels and blueschist facies are associated with which pressure and temperature conditions, respectively?
options: high temperature, low pressure and high pressure, low temperature
high temperature, high pressure and high pressure, low temperature
moderate temperature, moderate pressure and high pressure, low temperature
high temperature, low pressure and high pressure, high temperature
high temperature, low pressure and moderate pressure, moderate temperature
quiz.why: Hornfels forms next to hot magma at shallow depth (high T, low P). Blueschist forms in cold subduction zones (high P, low T).

quiz.q: Blueschist metamorphism is associated with what type of plate boundary?
options: ocean crust subducting beneath a continent
quiz.why: Blueschist forms in the cold, high-pressure setting of a subducting slab (trench and accretionary prism).

quiz.q: You walk away from a granite pluton across a contact aureole. What do you expect to find as you move outward?
options: Metamorphic grade increases away from the pluton
Metamorphic grade decreases, from high-grade hornfels toward unmetamorphosed rock
quiz.why: The heat source is the pluton. Grade is highest at the contact and falls with distance, as shown by the zones labelled high-grade, intermediate and low-grade hornfels.

quiz.q: A fault cuts through rock at two depths, 5 km and 20 km. Which pair of rocks forms at those depths?
options: Fault breccia at 5 km and mylonite at 20 km
Mylonite at 5 km and fault breccia at 20 km
Marble at 5 km and quartzite at 20 km
quiz.why: From 0 to 15 km rock is brittle and crushes to fault breccia. Below 15 km it is ductile and smears into mylonite.

quiz.q: Which type of metamorphism produces more metamorphic rock than any other mechanism?
quiz.why: Orogenesis (collisions) deforms and heats huge mobile belts hundreds to thousands of km long.

quiz.q: Pressure rises about 270 to 300 bars per km. About how much pressure would you expect at 10 km depth?
quiz.why: 10 km times 270 to 300 bars per km gives 2,700 to 3,000 bars (2.7 to 3 kbar), close to the low end of the typical 2 to 12 kbar range.

quiz.q:
Which of the following settings are matched to the correct metamorphism?
I. Heating by a plutonic intrusion: thermal (contact)
II. High P and low T alteration: subduction
III. Shearing in a fault zone: dynamic
quiz.why: All three settings match the standard list of metamorphism types.

quiz.q: Why do many exhumed high-grade metamorphic rocks keep their high-temperature minerals instead of changing back as they rise and cool?
options: They rise too quickly to be eroded
They are always melted again at the surface
Many are dry, which prevents retrograde reactions
quiz.why: Many metamorphic rocks are dry, which prevents retrograde reactions (changes back to low-grade minerals).

quiz.q: For a shale protolith, which list gives index minerals in order of increasing metamorphic grade?
quiz.why: The chart for pelitic (shale) rock runs from chlorite at low grade, through muscovite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, to sillimanite at high grade.

quiz.q: A geologist finds sillimanite in a rock from a shale protolith. What does this tell you?
options: The rock was only slightly metamorphosed (low grade)
The rock is a fault breccia
The rock reached high metamorphic grade
quiz.why: Index minerals show grade. Sillimanite sits at the highest-grade end of the pelitic chart, with gneiss.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched to its setting?
options: Dynamic metamorphism: shearing in a fault zone
Shock metamorphism: heat and low pressure from a deep pluton
Hydrothermal metamorphism: hot water alteration at ridges
Subduction metamorphism: high P and low T
quiz.why: Shock metamorphism is caused by extreme high pressure from a bolide impact (comet or asteroid), not by a deep pluton.
